grammarNote: Uses estar (temporary state), not ser. Standard informal greeting.
Literally 'of nothing.'
Llamarse is reflexive: me llamo = I call myself.
Informal. Llamarse is reflexive; literally 'how do you call yourself?'
Location uses estar, not ser.

englishVariants: I don't speak Spanish very well.

grammarNote: Spanish uses tener + noun (I have hunger), not ser/estar + adjective as in English.
Tener + noun idiom: literally 'I have thirst.'
Tener + noun: literally 'I have cold.' Contrast with hace frío (the weather is cold).
Tener + noun: literally 'I have heat.'
Origin and nationality use ser, not estar.
Temporary states use estar. Cansado is a condition, not a permanent trait.
Gustar is backwards from English: the coffee pleases me (el café = subject, me = indirect object pronoun).
Plural subject (películas) requires plural verb gustan.
Negation goes before the indirect object pronoun: no me gusta.
Weather uses hacer + noun: hace calor, hace frío, hace sol, hace viento.
Hacer for weather; afuera = outside. Never 'está frío' for weather.
Use son for all hours except one (es la una).
Querer + infinitive is a direct verb chain, similar to English 'want to.'
Me (indirect object pronoun) precedes the conjugated verb.

english: I'm going to go to the market.
grammarNote: Ir a + infinitive expresses near future. Al = a + el (contraction).
Tener que + infinitive expresses obligation.
Acabar de + infinitive = to have just done something (immediate past).
Deber + infinitive expresses moral obligation or duty.

spanish: Puedo hablar un poco de español.
english: I can speak a little Spanish.
grammarNote: Poder + infinitive = to be able to. Un poco de = a little of.

english: I'm going to call you tonight.
grammarNote: Ir a + infinitive for near future. Object pronoun (te) attaches to the infinitive.
Volver a + infinitive = to do something again. More idiomatic than adding 'otra vez.'
Dejar de + infinitive = to stop doing something.
Doler works like gustar: the head hurts me (la cabeza = subject, me = indirect object).
Faltar works like gustar: two dollars are lacking to me. Plural subject = plural verb.
Parecer works like gustar. Used to hedge opinions politely.
Encantar works like gustar. Plural subject (tacos) = plural verb (encantan).
Estar + gerund forms the present progressive. Used for actions happening right now.
Estar + gerund for weather in progress. Lloviendo = gerund of llover.

english: I'm still working on the project.
grammarNote: Seguir + gerund = to keep doing / to still be doing something.

spanish: El banco está a dos cuadras.
english: The bank is two blocks away.
grammarNote: Location uses estar, not ser.

spanish: La reunión es a las nueve.
grammarNote: Scheduled events use ser, not estar. This surprises learners who expect location/time to always use estar.
Origin uses ser: soy de + place. Never estar de for origin.
Cerrado (closed) is a resulting state, so estar is used.
Estar is used for how food tastes (a condition experienced in the moment). Ser rico = to be wealthy.
Spanish requires double negatives: no + verb + nada. Both no and nada are needed.

english: I never go to the gym.
grammarNote: Nunca can precede the verb without 'no.' If it follows: no voy nunca al gimnasio (double negative).
No + hay + nadie: double negative required in Spanish.

english: I don't want to go either.
grammarNote: Tampoco = neither/not either. Can precede verb without additional 'no.'
Para indicates the recipient/beneficiary of something.

english: I work for a large company.
grammarNote: Para indicates employment — working in service of an entity.
Por expresses gratitude for something received or done.

english: I did it for you (because of you).
englishVariants: I did it for your sake.
grammarNote: Por expresses motive or cause (on account of). Para would mean 'for your benefit/use.'
Por is used for means of transportation or communication.
Para indicates destination when traveling.

englishVariants: I wake up at seven o'clock.
grammarNote: Despertarse is reflexive: the action reflects back on the subject.
Bañarse (reflexive) = to bathe oneself. Bañar (non-reflexive) = to bathe someone else.
Sentirse (reflexive) = to feel (emotionally/physically). Sentar = to seat someone.
Acordarse de (reflexive) = to remember. Requires de before the object.
Tener razón = to be right. English uses 'to be'; Spanish uses 'to have.'
Age uses tener in Spanish (I have 28 years), not ser/estar as in English.
Tener prisa = to be in a hurry. Literally 'I have hurry.'
Tener miedo de = to be afraid of. Literally 'I have fear of.'
Tener ganas de + infinitive = to feel like doing something.
Tener sueño = to be sleepy. Literally 'to have sleep.'
Despacio = slowly. Más despacio = more slowly.

english: How do you say 'umbrella' in Spanish?
grammarNote: Impersonal se: how is 'umbrella' said in Spanish? One of the most useful learner phrases.
Impersonal se + verb for general rules/prohibitions. No subject is specified.
Passive se construction: se + third person verb for general/impersonal statements.
Impersonal se: how is it written?
Hay que + infinitive = impersonal obligation (one must). No subject is specified.
Pasar is used impersonally: what is happening to you? Very common colloquial expression.
Common reassurance phrase. Literally 'nothing is happening.'
A lo mejor expresses possibility but takes indicative, not subjunctive (unlike quizás/tal vez).
Caer bien = to make a good impression. Distinct from gustar (preference or attraction).
Ya no = no longer. Ya (already/now) + no creates this compound negation.
Todavía no + present perfect = haven't done something yet.

spanish: Hace dos años que vivo aquí.
english: I've been living here for two years.
grammarNote: Hace + time + que + present tense = duration of an ongoing action. English uses present perfect; Spanish uses present.

english: How long have you been in Mexico?
grammarNote: Llevar + time = how long have you been... Same structure as llevar + gerund.

spanish: Se tarda una hora en llegar.
english: It takes an hour to get there.
grammarNote: Impersonal se + tardar to express duration of travel or process.

english: How did it go for you?
grammarNote: Ir + indirect object pronoun to ask how something went for someone.
De acuerdo is a noun phrase; estar de acuerdo = to be in agreement (a state).

spanish: La fiesta es en mi casa.
english: The party is at my house.
grammarNote: Events use ser for location (where something takes place). A classic exception to 'location = estar.'
Ser listo = to be clever. Estar listo = to be ready. Meaning changes with ser vs. estar.
Estar listo = to be ready (a state). Ser listo = to be clever.
Ser malo = to be bad/evil (character). Estar malo = to be sick or taste bad.

spanish: Me lo dijeron la semana pasada.
grammarNote: Me (indirect) + lo (direct) before the verb. When two pronouns co-occur, indirect comes first.
Te (indirect) + lo (direct) before the verb.

english: I sent it to him/her yesterday.
grammarNote: Le becomes se when followed by lo/la/los/las to avoid two l-pronouns.
With affirmative commands, object pronouns attach to the end: da + me + lo.
With negative commands, pronouns go before the verb: no + me + lo + digas.
Direct object pronoun can precede estar or attach to the gerund: estoy pensándolo.
Se replaces le before lo. A ella is added for clarity since se is ambiguous.

english: I'm going to buy it for you.
grammarNote: With infinitives, pronouns attach: voy a comprar + te + lo. Accent mark added to maintain stress.
Accidental/unplanned events: se + indirect object + verb. Literally 'the book forgot itself to me.' Subject is el libro.
Accidental construction: se + me + cayó. Removes personal blame; literally 'the glass fell to me.'
Accidental se: the phone lost itself on me. Implies it was unintentional.
Accidental se: the glass broke itself to me. Implies it was unintentional.
Se + nos + acabó: accidental construction. Literally 'time finished itself on us.'

spanish: Se les olvidó traer el dinero.
english: They forgot to bring the money.
grammarNote: Accidental se + les (third person plural). Literally 'the money forgot itself to them.'
Passive se with plural subject: frutas is plural, so the verb is plural (se venden).

spanish: Lo que más me gusta es la música.
english: What I like most is music.
grammarNote: Lo que + relative clause creates a nominal clause (what I like). Lo is a neuter article here.
Se me hace tarde = it's getting late for me. Idiomatic use of hacerse (to become).
Ponerse + adjective = to become (emotional or physical change). One of several 'to become' verbs in Spanish.
Casarse (reflexive) = to get married. Often used reciprocally with plural subjects.
Equivocarse de = to be wrong about / to get the wrong thing. Always reflexive.

spanish: Se queja mucho de su trabajo.
english: He/she complains a lot about work.
grammarNote: Quejarse (reflexive) = to complain. Always requires reflexive pronoun.

spanish: Me di cuenta de que estaba equivocado.
grammarNote: Darse cuenta de = to realize/notice. Not 'realizar' (a false friend). Equivocado uses estar.
Extrañar is the preferred verb for 'to miss' in Latin America. Spain uses echar de menos.
Valer la pena = to be worth it. Literally 'to be worth the trouble.'

english: It turns out they were right.
grammarNote: Resulta que + indicative = it turns out that. Used to introduce surprising information.

english: I don't care. / It's all the same to me.
grammarNote: Dar igual = to be all the same to someone (indifference). Me da lo mismo is equivalent.
¿Qué tal? is an informal way to ask 'how is/are...?'
Reflexive reciprocal: we see each other. Common farewell.
Used when passing by or leaving. Distinct from perdón (apology or bumping into someone).
Estar is used for conditions/states resulting from a change (included = a resulting condition).

english: What time does the bus leave?

grammarNote: Being lost is a state: estar is used.

english: How do I get to downtown?
englishVariants: How do I get to the city center?
grammarNote: Llegar a = to arrive at / to get to.
Siga is the formal imperative of seguir. Todo derecho = straight ahead.
Formal imperative of doblar. A la izquierda = to the left.

english: How long does it take to get there?
grammarNote: Tardar en + infinitive = to take (time) to do something.

english: I've been waiting for three hours.
grammarNote: Llevar + time + gerund = to have been doing something for a duration. No equivalent in English uses this structure.
Ir + gerund expresses movement while performing an action.
Seguir sin + infinitive = to still not be doing something.

english: They've been married for twenty years.
grammarNote: Llevar + time + past participle (used as adjective) expresses duration of a state.
Andar + gerund = to be going around doing something (implies ongoing, sometimes aimless activity). Informal.

english: I've been going days without sleeping well.
grammarNote: Llevar + time + sin + infinitive = to have been without doing something for a duration.

spanish: Espero que tengas un buen día.
english: I hope you have a good day.
grammarNote: Esperar que triggers subjunctive. Different subjects in each clause require subjunctive.

english: I want you to come with me.
grammarNote: Querer que + subjunctive when subjects differ. English uses infinitive; Spanish requires subjunctive.

spanish: Es importante que llegues a tiempo.
english: It's important that you arrive on time.
grammarNote: Impersonal expressions (es importante que) trigger subjunctive in the dependent clause.
No creer que triggers subjunctive (negated belief = doubt). Creer que (affirmative) uses indicative.
Ojalá always triggers subjunctive. One of few words requiring subjunctive without a 'que' clause.
Tal vez + subjunctive expresses uncertainty. Tal vez + indicative expresses more certainty.
Cuando + subjunctive for future events. Cuando + indicative for habitual/past events.
Alegrarse de que triggers subjunctive. Emotional reaction to another's action requires subjunctive.
Dudar que triggers subjunctive (expression of doubt).

spanish: Es una lástima que no puedas venir.
english: It's a shame you can't come.
grammarNote: Impersonal emotional expression + que triggers subjunctive.

spanish: Busco un apartamento que tenga dos habitaciones.
english: I'm looking for an apartment that has two bedrooms.
grammarNote: Non-specific/hypothetical antecedent triggers subjunctive in the relative clause.

spanish: Quisiera reservar una mesa para dos.
english: I'd like to reserve a table for two.
grammarNote: Quisiera (imperfect subjunctive of querer) is a polite softener instead of quiero.

spanish: Para que lo sepas, ya terminé.
english: Just so you know, I already finished.
grammarNote: Para que always triggers subjunctive (purpose clause with different subjects).

english: Even if it's difficult, I'll try.
grammarNote: Aunque + subjunctive concedes an unknown/hypothetical condition. Aunque + indicative = even though (known fact).

english: Take care! / I hope things go well for you!
grammarNote: Que + subjunctive = may things go well for you. Indirect wish without a main verb.
Que + subjunctive = may you enjoy it. Fixed expression said before or during a meal.

spanish: Que yo sepa, no hay problema.
english: As far as I know, there's no problem.
grammarNote: Que yo sepa uses present subjunctive in an independent clause to express limited knowledge.
Querer in subjunctive after lo que creates a free relative clause (whatever you want).
Real/open condition: si + present indicative + future indicative.

spanish: Si tuviera dinero, viajaría por el mundo.
english: If I had money, I would travel the world.
grammarNote: Hypothetical si clause: si + imperfect subjunctive (tuviera) + conditional (viajaría).

english: If I could, I would help you.
grammarNote: Hypothetical: si + imperfect subjunctive (pudiera) + conditional (ayudaría).

spanish: Si fuera rico, compraría una isla.
english: If I were rich, I'd buy an island.
grammarNote: Hypothetical: si + imperfect subjunctive (fuera) + conditional (compraría).

english: What would you do if you lost your job?
grammarNote: Hypothetical question: si + imperfect subjunctive (perdieras) + conditional (harías).

spanish: Si estuvieras aquí, todo sería diferente.
english: If you were here, everything would be different.
grammarNote: Hypothetical: si + imperfect subjunctive (estuvieras) + conditional (sería).

spanish: Si hubiera llegado antes, habría visto el show.
english: If I had arrived earlier, I would have seen the show.
grammarNote: Past counterfactual: si + past perfect subjunctive (hubiera llegado) + conditional perfect (habría visto).

english: If I had known, I would have come.
grammarNote: Past counterfactual: si + past perfect subjunctive + conditional perfect.

spanish: De haberlo sabido, no habría ido.
english: Had I known, I wouldn't have gone.
grammarNote: De + perfect infinitive (haberlo sabido) can replace si + past perfect subjunctive in formal registers.
Ni siquiera una idea = not even one idea. Ni used as an emphatic negation intensifier.

spanish: No vino ni siquiera a llamar.
english: He didn't even bother to call.
grammarNote: Ni siquiera = not even. Emphatic negation.

spanish: No quiero ni café ni té.
english: I don't want either coffee or tea.
englishVariants: I want neither coffee nor tea.
grammarNote: Ni...ni = neither...nor. Requires no before the verb when the construction follows it.
Jamás = never (stronger than nunca, often emphatic or permanent).

english: I never said that. / At no point did I say that.
grammarNote: Ningún + noun before the verb can stand alone. After the verb: no dije eso en ningún momento (double negative).
Más after a negated verb = any more. No more.
Para qué = for what purpose. Por qué = why (for what reason).

spanish: Lo cambié por uno más nuevo.
english: I exchanged it for a newer one.
grammarNote: Por indicates exchange. Para would indicate destination or purpose.
Por indicates movement through or along a place.

english: For a beginner, you speak well.
grammarNote: Para + noun/infinitive expresses 'considering' or an unexpected contrast.

spanish: El informe debe estar listo para el lunes.
english: The report must be ready by Monday.
grammarNote: Para is used for deadlines.
Interesar works like gustar. Le = third person indirect object.
Molestar works like gustar: the noise bothers us (el ruido = subject, nos = indirect object).

english: Do you mind if I open the window?
grammarNote: Importar works like gustar: does it matter to you? Te = second person indirect object.

englishVariants: It costs him/her a lot of effort.
grammarNote: Costar works like gustar for expressing difficulty.

english: I find it hard to believe.
grammarNote: Costar + infinitive = to be hard (for someone) to do. Works like gustar: it costs me to believe it.

english: It's our turn to pay this time.
grammarNote: Tocar works like gustar: it falls to us to pay. Used for turns and obligations falling to someone.

english: Do you have time to spare?
grammarNote: Sobrar works like gustar: does time remain over for you? Opposite of faltar.

english: He/she urgently needs to find work.
grammarNote: Urgir works like gustar: finding work is urgent to him/her.
Preocupar works like gustar: that thing worries me. Me = indirect object, eso = subject.

spanish: Tengo la impresión de que algo falla.
english: I have the impression that something is wrong.
grammarNote: Tener la impresión de que = to have the impression that. Combines tener-expression with a noun clause.

spanish: No tengo ni tiempo ni dinero.
english: I have neither time nor money.
grammarNote: Combines tener-expression with ni...ni construction.
Tener entendido que = to understand/have heard that (based on prior information).
Tomar el pelo = to pull someone's leg/tease. Me = indirect object; progressive form with estar.

english: How cool! / What a great vibe!
grammarNote: Buena onda (good wave/vibe) is widely used in Mexico and other Latin American countries.
Por fin = finally/at last.

spanish: Sin embargo, creo que tienes razón.
grammarNote: Sin embargo = however/nevertheless. Formal discourse connector.

spanish: A pesar de eso, lo intenté.
grammarNote: A pesar de = despite / in spite of. Followed by noun or infinitive.

spanish: Al fin y al cabo, todo salió bien.
english: In the end, everything turned out well.
englishVariants: After all, everything turned out fine.
grammarNote: Al fin y al cabo = in the end/after all. Discourse marker for a conclusion.
Tener en cuenta = to bear in mind / to take into account.
Llevar a cabo = to carry out / to accomplish. Fixed idiom.

english: To be up to date on something.
grammarNote: Estar al tanto de = to be in the know/up to date. Uses estar for the current state of awareness.
Discourse marker used to pause and think. Written a ver (not haber).
Very common discourse filler in spoken Spanish, especially among younger speakers.

englishVariants: All of a sudden they appeared.
grammarNote: De repente = suddenly. Common adverbial phrase.
De hecho = in fact/actually. Used to confirm or add supporting information.
A tiempo = on time. Not the same as en tiempo (in time/in season).

english: No way! / Out of the question!
grammarNote: Literally 'not even speaking.' Used as emphatic refusal or disbelief.
Literally 'there's nothing to thank for.' Alternative to de nada.

spanish: Estar a la vuelta de la esquina.
grammarNote: Spatial expression often used idiomatically to mean something is very close or about to happen.
Claro que sí = clearly yes. Very common affirmation.

spanish: Quiero que me digan la verdad.
english: I want them to tell me the truth.
grammarNote: Querer que + subjunctive (digan) with different subjects. Me = indirect object pronoun in the dependent clause.
Esperar que + present perfect subjunctive (hayas descansado) for completed actions.

spanish: Quería que vinieras a la fiesta.
english: I wanted you to come to the party.
grammarNote: Past tense main verb (quería) + past subjunctive (vinieras) when subjects differ.

spanish: No había nadie que supiera la respuesta.
english: There was nobody who knew the answer.
grammarNote: Negative antecedent in past (no había nadie) triggers past subjunctive in the relative clause.

spanish: A menos que vengas tú, no hay quórum.
english: Unless you come, there's no quorum.
grammarNote: A menos que always triggers subjunctive. It expresses a conditional exception.

spanish: Antes de que te vayas, necesito decirte algo.
english: Before you leave, I need to tell you something.
grammarNote: Antes de que always triggers subjunctive (future event, different subject).

spanish: Con tal de que llegues a tiempo, todo está bien.
english: As long as you arrive on time, everything is fine.
grammarNote: Con tal de que triggers subjunctive. It expresses a condition for acceptability.

english: Whenever I can, I'll help you.
grammarNote: Siempre que = whenever/as long as, followed by subjunctive for habitual future conditions.

english: He talks as if he knew everything.
grammarNote: Como si always triggers imperfect subjunctive (presents something as hypothetical/unreal).

spanish: No hay nadie que lo sepa.
english: There's no one who knows it.
grammarNote: Negative antecedent (no hay nadie) triggers subjunctive in the relative clause.

english: I wish I could go with you.
grammarNote: Ojalá + imperfect subjunctive expresses an unlikely or impossible wish in the present/future.

english: I wish I had been able to help you.
grammarNote: Ojalá + past perfect subjunctive expresses regret about something that didn't happen.

spanish: Pase lo que pase, estaré aquí.
grammarNote: Pase lo que pase = whatever happens. Concessive subjunctive construction.

spanish: Hagas lo que hagas, apoyaré tu decisión.
english: Whatever you do, I'll support your decision.
grammarNote: Concessive subjunctive with repetition (hagas lo que hagas) = whatever you do.

spanish: Por más que lo intento, no lo logro.
english: No matter how hard I try, I can't manage it.
grammarNote: Por más que + subjunctive/indicative = no matter how much. Expresses futile effort.
Servirle (indirect object pronoun attached to infinitive). Used in formal/service contexts.

english: It would have been better to tell him before.
grammarNote: Conditional perfect (habría sido) for an action that didn't happen. Decírselo = decir + se + lo attached.

spanish: Lo que me molesta es la hipocresía.
grammarNote: Lo que + clause = nominalized relative clause used as subject. Lo is a neuter article.

english: The more you practice, the better you speak.
grammarNote: Mientras más...más/mejor is the Latin American correlative construction for 'the more...the more.'

spanish: Fue entonces cuando lo entendí todo.
english: It was then that I understood everything.
grammarNote: Cleft sentence: fue + time expression + cuando. Used for emphasis. Ser acts as a linking verb.

spanish: Lo que me sorprende es tu actitud.
english: What surprises me is your attitude.
grammarNote: Lo que + clause = what (nominalized relative). Acts as subject of the main clause.
Hacerse + noun/adjective = to become. Se hizo de noche = it became night. Impersonal.

english: The sooner you do it, the better.
grammarNote: Cuanto antes = the sooner. This correlative structure differs from mientras más...más.

spanish: No me parece que sea la mejor opción.
english: It doesn't seem to me that it's the best option.
grammarNote: No parecer que triggers subjunctive (negated verb of seeming introduces doubt).
Arrepentirse de (reflexive) = to regret. Followed by perfect infinitive (haber + past participle).

spanish: Se atrevió a decirle la verdad.
english: He/she dared to tell him/her the truth.
grammarNote: Atreverse a + infinitive = to dare to do something. Always reflexive.

spanish: Me enamoré de ella a primera vista.
english: I fell in love with her at first sight.
grammarNote: Enamorarse de (reflexive) = to fall in love with. A primera vista = at first sight.
Irse (reflexive) = to leave/go away. Despedirse (reflexive) = to say goodbye. Sin + infinitive.
Llevarse bien/mal = to get along well/poorly. Reciprocal reflexive.

spanish: Se negó a hablar con la prensa.
english: He/she refused to speak to the press.
grammarNote: Negarse a + infinitive = to refuse to do. Always reflexive.
Ponerse de acuerdo = to reach agreement. Ponerse + noun/adj phrase for 'becoming' in a state.
Preocuparse (reflexive) = to worry. Negative informal command: no + te + preocupes (subjunctive form).

spanish: ¿En qué se diferencia esto de aquello?
english: How does this differ from that?
englishVariants: What's the difference between this and that?
grammarNote: Diferenciarse de (reflexive) = to differ from. ¿En qué? = in what way?

englishVariants: He/she is on the verge of arriving.
grammarNote: Estar por + infinitive = to be about to do something (near future).

english: I can't manage to understand this concept.
grammarNote: Lograr + infinitive = to manage to do / to succeed in doing. Useful alternative to poder.

english: He took an hour to reply.
grammarNote: Tardar + time + en + infinitive = to take (time) to do something.
Tratar de + infinitive = to try to do. No before the infinitive = try not to.
Alegrarse de + infinitive = to be glad to do. When subjects are the same, use infinitive (not subjunctive).
Acabar de + infinitive in third person = he/she just did something.
Me + verb in third person plural = passive/impersonal event done to me. Common for victimization.
Le = indirect object pronoun. Pasar a alguien = to happen to someone.

english: The power went out on me.
grammarNote: Accidental se + indirect object: something happened to me involuntarily. Literally 'the power left itself to me.'

spanish: Dicho esto, pasemos al siguiente tema.
english: That said, let's move on to the next topic.
grammarNote: Absolute participial construction: dicho esto = having said this. No conjugated verb in the participial phrase.

spanish: Se empezó a entender la situación.
english: The situation began to be understood.
grammarNote: Empezar a + infinitive with impersonal se creates a passive-like construction.

english: When do you want me to do it?
grammarNote: Querer que + subjunctive (haga) with different subjects.

english: I hope to be able to see you soon.
grammarNote: Esperar + infinitive (same subject) vs. esperar que + subjunctive (different subjects).

spanish: Se me hace agua la boca.
grammarNote: Hacerse agua la boca = my mouth waters. Idiomatic use of hacerse with body part + indirect object.

english: To put one's foot in it. / To mess up.
grammarNote: Meter la pata = to stick one's paw in = to make a social or practical blunder.
Echar de menos = to miss a person or place. Preferred in Spain; Latin America uses extrañar.

english: To ruin something. / To spoil something.
grammarNote: Echar a perder = to throw to waste = to ruin. Reflexive form echarse a perder = to go bad (food).

spanish: No tener pelos en la lengua.
english: To be outspoken. / To not mince words.
grammarNote: Literally 'to have no hairs on the tongue' = to speak bluntly without filtering.

spanish: A que no sabes qué me pasó.
english: I bet you don't know what happened to me.
grammarNote: A que + negation = I bet (introducing something the speaker thinks the listener doesn't know). Very colloquial.

spanish: Resulta que me lo dijeron mal.
english: It turns out they told me wrong.
grammarNote: Resultar que + indicative = it turns out that. Common frame for surprising revelations.
Mexican expression of enthusiasm. Padre = father, but colloquially means 'cool/awesome.'
Common Latin American expression of resignation or refusal depending on context.

spanish: En cambio, mi hermano sí fue.
english: On the other hand, my brother did go.
grammarNote: En cambio = on the other hand / instead. Introduces a contrasting idea.
A veces = sometimes. Sentirse solo = to feel lonely (reflexive verb + adjective).
En realidad = actually/in reality. Doesn't carry the contradictory force of 'actually' in English.

english: By the way, did you see the news?
grammarNote: A propósito = by the way (to introduce a new topic).

spanish: En cuanto a eso, no sé.
english: As for that, I don't know.
grammarNote: En cuanto a = as for / regarding. Used to frame a topic.

spanish: Siento que hayas tenido que esperar.
english: I'm sorry you had to wait.
grammarNote: Sentir que + present perfect subjunctive for regret about a completed event.

spanish: No lo haré sin que me lo pidas.
english: I won't do it unless you ask me.
grammarNote: Sin que triggers subjunctive (different subjects required).

spanish: Busca a alguien que hable chino.
english: He's looking for someone who speaks Chinese.
grammarNote: Indefinite/unknown antecedent (someone hypothetical) triggers subjunctive in the relative clause.
Que + subjunctive (bendiga) expresses a wish or blessing. Indirect command/wish without main verb.

spanish: Aunque hubiera querido, no habría podido.
english: Even if I had wanted to, I wouldn't have been able to.
grammarNote: Aunque + past perfect subjunctive (hubiera querido) + conditional perfect (habría podido).

spanish: Me temo que no va a funcionar.
english: I'm afraid it's not going to work.
grammarNote: Temerse (reflexive) = to be afraid/suspect (used to hedge bad news). Different nuance from tener miedo.

english: What do you recommend to me?
grammarNote: Me = indirect object pronoun. Recomendar is a verb like gustar in that it needs an indirect object.

english: Can you explain it to me?
grammarNote: Me (indirect) + lo (direct) before the modal verb. Can also attach to the infinitive: ¿puedes explicármelo?
Nos (indirect) + lo (direct) before the verb. Todo = everything (direct object not replaced by lo here).

spanish: ¿Por qué no nos tomamos un descanso?
english: Why don't we take a break?
grammarNote: Tomarse un descanso (reflexive) = to take a break for oneself. ¿Por qué no + present? = invitation.
Pelearse (reflexive/reciprocal) = to fight/argue with each other.

spanish: Estaba tan cansado que me dormí en el sofá.
english: I was so tired that I fell asleep on the sofa.
grammarNote: Dormirse (reflexive) = to fall asleep (involuntary). Dormir = to sleep (general activity).

spanish: No quiero ni café ni té.
english: I don't want either coffee or tea.
englishVariants: I want neither coffee nor tea.
grammarNote: Ni...ni = neither...nor. Requires no before the verb when the construction follows it.

spanish: No lo ha visto nadie todavía.
grammarNote: Double negative: no + verb + nadie. Nadie after the verb adds emphasis. Todavía = yet/still.

english: I had never seen anything like that.
grammarNote: Jamás + past perfect = had never. Algo here becomes 'anything' in a negative context.
Ningún + masculine singular noun as emphatic negation. Double negative: no + verb + ningún.

english: I will never ever do it.
grammarNote: Nunca jamás = never ever. Double negative adverbs for maximum emphasis.

spanish: Por nada del mundo lo diría.
english: I wouldn't say it for anything in the world.
grammarNote: Por nada del mundo = not for anything in the world. Emphatic negation with conditional.

spanish: Hace un calor de muerte hoy.
grammarNote: Hacer + noun + de muerte = idiomatic intensification of weather expressions.

english: At nightfall it started to rain.
englishVariants: When night fell, it started to rain.
grammarNote: Al + infinitive = upon/when doing something. Al anochecer = when night fell (anochecer = to get dark).

english: One would need to study more.
grammarNote: Habría que + infinitive = conditional impersonal obligation. The conditional form of hay que.
Conditional perfect of poder (podría haber) + past participle = could have done.

english: He/she should have said it earlier.
grammarNote: Deber in conditional (debería) + haber + past participle = should have done.
Que + subjunctive in an independent clause expresses a wish. The que is mandatory.

spanish: No por mucho madrugar amanece más temprano.
english: Getting up earlier doesn't make the sun rise sooner. / Haste makes waste.
grammarNote: Proverb: rushing doesn't speed up natural outcomes. Madrugar = to rise early. Amanecer = for dawn to break.

english: Don't pay attention to foolish words.
englishVariants: Turn a deaf ear to foolishness.
grammarNote: Proverb using ellipsis: to foolish words, deaf ears. Shows how Spanish proverbs omit verbs.
Cada quien = each one. A lo suyo = to their own thing. Expresses non-interference.
Absolute participle construction: said and done. Common expression showing efficiency.

spanish: Cueste lo que cueste, lo terminaré.
english: Whatever it costs, I'll finish it.
englishVariants: No matter what it costs, I'll finish it.
grammarNote: Cueste lo que cueste = concessive subjunctive construction (whatever it costs). Expresses unconditional commitment.

english: Desperate times call for desperate measures.
grammarNote: Proverb: to great problems, great remedies. Illustrates Spanish proverbs' parallel prepositional structure.
